quiz.explanation: No lender is charging interest, but the money could have been distributed to owners or used elsewhere, and that forgone alternative is its cost. Whether it is dearer than a loan depends on the returns available, and dividends are what retention avoids paying.

quiz.question: Why is retained profit unavailable to most start-up businesses?
options: Regulations prevent new firms from using it
Their shareholders always demand dividends
Banks require it to be held as security
They have not yet made any profit to retain
quiz.explanation: Retained profit comes from trading that has already happened, so a business that has not yet traded profitably has nothing to keep. There is no rule against it, and the constraint is the absence of profit rather than any demand on it.

quiz.question: A business sells a delivery van it no longer needs after moving to a contracted distributor. This is best described as:
options: Sale of assets, an internal source
An external source of finance
A form of trade credit from a supplier
Sale and leaseback of a fixed asset
quiz.explanation: The value was already inside the business and selling only changes the form it is held in, which is what makes sale of assets internal. Sale and leaseback would mean renting the van back afterwards, which is not what happened here.

quiz.question: In the specification's terms, a business angel is best described as:
options: A method of finance
A source of finance
A form of business
A type of business plan
quiz.explanation: A source is the party the money comes from, and an angel is a person providing it. The shares the angel receives are the method — the form the finance takes — which is the distinction the chapter opens with.

quiz.question: Which of these is a method of finance rather than a source?
options: Family and friends
A peer-to-peer platform
Trade credit
Other businesses
quiz.explanation: Trade credit is an arrangement under which the money arrives, which is what the specification calls a method. The other three are all parties providing finance, which makes them sources.

quiz.question: Peer-to-peer funding differs from equity crowd funding because peer-to-peer funding:
options: Gives backers a reward or early product
Is only available to listed companies
Requires security over a business asset
Is lending that must be repaid with interest
quiz.explanation: Peer-to-peer matches a business with many individual lenders, and lending is repaid with interest whoever provides it. Rewards and early products belong to reward-based crowd funding, and equity crowd funding gives shares instead.

quiz.question: A business needs to cover a six-week gap between paying suppliers and being paid by customers. The most suitable method is:
options: An overdraft facility
A five-year bank loan
A share issue to investors
A government grant
quiz.explanation: An overdraft is designed for a short, uncertain shortfall and charges interest only on what is used and only while it is used. A five-year loan commits the business far beyond the need, and a share issue or grant could not be arranged in the time.

quiz.question: A loan of $90,000 is repaid at $1,800 a month for 5 years. The total interest paid is:
quiz.explanation: The total repaid is $1,800 times 60 months, or $108,000, and the interest is whatever that exceeds the sum borrowed: $108,000 less $90,000 gives $18,000. The total repaid and the amount borrowed are the two inputs, not the answer.

quiz.question: A machine costs $40,000 to buy, or $900 a month to lease for 48 months. Leasing costs:
options: $3,200 less than buying
exactly the same as buying
$3,200 more than buying
$40,000 more than buying
quiz.explanation: The lease payments come to $900 times 48, which is $43,200, against a purchase price of $40,000 — a premium of $3,200. What that buys is the avoidance of a large payment at the start.

quiz.question: The main advantage of trade credit as a method of finance is that it:
options: Provides a large sum for buying assets
Guarantees a discount on every order
Cannot be withdrawn by the supplier
Is interest-free while the credit period runs
quiz.explanation: A supplier agreeing to be paid later lets the business hold and sell stock before cash leaves, at no interest cost. Discounts are usually offered for paying early rather than late, and a supplier can shorten or withdraw terms.

quiz.question: A grant differs from every other method of external finance because it:
options: Does not have to be repaid
Arrives faster than any other method
Can be spent on anything the firm chooses
Is available to any business that applies
quiz.explanation: A grant is money the business keeps without repaying and without issuing shares for it, which no other method offers. Grants are typically slow and competitive, and are restricted to the purpose they were awarded for.

quiz.question: A founder holding all 120,000 shares issues 30,000 new shares to an investor. The founder now holds:
quiz.explanation: The founder still holds 120,000 shares, but there are now 150,000 in issue, so the stake is 120,000 divided by 150,000, which is 80%. The investor holds the remaining 20%.

quiz.question: Which circumstance most strongly favours equity finance over a bank loan?
options: The business has valuable assets to offer
The owner wants to keep full control
The business has no trading history yet
The business needs the money within days
quiz.explanation: A lender wants evidence of repayment and something to secure the debt against, so a business with neither must find a provider paid by growth instead. Assets and a wish to keep control both point the other way, towards borrowing.

quiz.question: Which form of business has a separate legal identity from its owners?
options: A sole trader
A general partnership
A lifestyle business
A private limited company
quiz.explanation: Incorporation creates a company that owns assets and owes debts in its own name, which is what separates it from its owners. A sole trader and a partnership are not separate in law, and a lifestyle business describes a purpose rather than a legal form.

quiz.question: A sole trader cannot raise finance by issuing shares because:
options: There is no company whose ownership divides into shares
The law caps the amount they may raise
Banks must approve any share issue first
Sole traders are not permitted to have investors
quiz.explanation: Shares are units of ownership in a company, and an unincorporated business has no company for them to be units of, so the method is closed until it incorporates. No cap or approval is involved, and a sole trader can take investment in other forms.

quiz.question: What is the key benefit of franchising for the franchisee?
options: Complete freedom over pricing and suppliers
An established brand and proven business model
No fees or royalties payable to the franchisor
Protection from the debts of the business
quiz.explanation: The franchisee starts with a name customers already recognise and a format that is known to work, which is what lowers the risk of opening. Fees and royalties are what is paid for that, and the franchisor sets prices, suppliers and appearance.

quiz.question: Franchising helps the franchisor raise finance because the network:
options: Qualifies for government start-up grants
Can be sold to investors more easily
Is funded by the franchisees' own capital
Avoids the need to register the brand
quiz.explanation: Each outlet is paid for by the operator opening it, so the brand expands without financing every site itself, which is why franchising appears in a topic about raising finance. Grants, resale and registration are unrelated to how the outlets are funded.

quiz.question: A social enterprise differs from a conventional business mainly because it:
options: Is not permitted to make any profit at all
Must be constituted as a public limited company
Relies entirely on donations rather than sales
Reinvests most of its surplus into a social aim
quiz.explanation: A social enterprise trades and earns revenue like any business; what differs is where the surplus goes, since most of it funds the purpose rather than the owners. It is not barred from surplus, can take various legal forms, and sells rather than relies on donations.

quiz.question: A company issues 150,000 new shares at $6 each at flotation. The amount raised is:
quiz.explanation: The sum raised is the number of new shares multiplied by the price each was sold for: 150,000 times $6 gives $900,000. The share count itself is an input to the calculation rather than its answer.

quiz.question: The key disadvantage of unlimited liability for a sole trader is that:
options: They cannot employ any members of staff
Their personal assets are at risk if it fails
They must publish their accounts each year
They pay a higher rate of tax on profits
quiz.explanation: The owner and the business are the same in law, so creditors can pursue savings, vehicles and in some cases the home. Publishing accounts is an obligation that comes with incorporating, and unlimited liability places no limit on employing staff.

quiz.question: Limited liability means a shareholder's maximum loss is:
options: The debts the company owes its creditors
A fixed proportion of the company's debts
The amount they paid for their shares
Their share of the company's annual losses
quiz.explanation: The company owes its own debts, so a shareholder risks only the money already handed over for the shares. The company's debts remain the company's, and a shareholder is not allocated a portion of them.

quiz.question: A bank lending to a small private company often requires a personal guarantee from the owner because:
options: The law requires a guarantee on every loan
A guarantee removes the need for any interest
Private companies cannot offer any security
Limited liability would otherwise cap its claim
quiz.explanation: Without one, the bank could claim only against the company, which may hold little; the guarantee puts the owner personally behind that one debt. It is a commercial requirement rather than a legal one, and it does not replace interest or other security.

quiz.question: A profitable partnership wants to raise substantial equity finance for expansion. It must first:
options: Incorporate as a limited company
Apply for a government development grant
Increase the number of partners it has
Repay its existing bank borrowing
quiz.explanation: Equity finance means selling shares, and only a company has ownership divided into shares to sell, so incorporation has to come first. Taking in more partners raises capital but is not equity finance in this sense, and neither grants nor repaying debt creates shares.

practice.question: Define the term 'retained profit'. (2 marks)
practice.guidance: Two marks for a definition with both halves. Profit remaining after tax and dividends have been paid (1 mark), which the business keeps to reinvest rather than distributing to its owners (1 mark). A definition naming only "profit kept by the business" has the idea but not the position in the profit figure, which is what the second mark is for.

practice.question: A business can buy a machine for $40,000 or lease it for $900 a month over 48 months. Calculate the additional cost of leasing rather than buying. (4 marks)
practice.guidance: Show the method, because the method is what is being assessed. Total lease cost = $900 × 48 months (1 mark) = $43,200 (1 mark). Additional cost = $43,200 − $40,000 (1 mark) = $3,200 (1 mark). An answer giving only the monthly figure has not compared anything; an answer giving $43,200 alone has stopped one step short of the question.

practice.question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for a technology start-up of using venture capital as a source of finance. (4 marks)
practice.guidance: Two developed points, each a reason taken to its consequence. Advantage: venture capital provides large sums to a business with no profits or assets to secure a loan against (1 mark), so development can be funded at a speed borrowing could not support (1 mark). Disadvantage: the fund takes a substantial shareholding and usually a say in decisions (1 mark), so the founders permanently give up part of the ownership and some control over the direction of the business (1 mark).

practice.question: A founder who owns all 120,000 shares in her company raises $60,000 by issuing 30,000 new shares to a business angel. Analyse the impact of this decision on the founder. (6 marks)
practice.guidance: Follow the chain rather than listing effects. The finance arrives without repayment or interest (1 mark), so the money can go into growth rather than into servicing a debt (1 mark). But shares in issue rise to 150,000 while the founder still holds 120,000 (1 mark), so her stake falls from 100% to 80% (1 mark). She therefore keeps every share but owns a smaller proportion of a business she now shares decisions over (1 mark), and any future issue dilutes her again (1 mark). Credit an answer that reaches the 80% figure from the share counts rather than asserting dilution.

practice.question: A profitable partnership running three restaurants plans to open ten more and needs finance it cannot generate itself. Assess whether it should incorporate as a private limited company. (10 marks)
practice.guidance: Levels-marked, so the judgement is what is assessed rather than the number of points made. The case for incorporating: only a company can issue shares, so equity finance — business angels, venture capital, investment from another business — is closed to the partnership as it stands, and an expansion of this size is unlikely to be funded from retained profit and secured borrowing alone. Limited liability also caps what the partners can lose, which matters when ten new sites are being committed to at once. The case against: incorporation costs money and time, accounts become public and readable by competitors, and a bank lending to a small new company will probably still want personal guarantees, which returns the partners to personal exposure for that debt. The strongest answers judge on which constraint actually binds this partnership — if the expansion can be funded by borrowing against the existing restaurants, the case is much weaker than if it cannot — and say so using the figures given rather than in general terms.

practice.question: Evaluate the view that a detailed business plan is the most important factor in determining whether a new business succeeds. (20 marks)
practice.guidance: Levels-marked and judged on the weighing, so no list of advantages and disadvantages will reach the top levels without a supported judgement. Build the case: the plan forces every assumption to be stated and costed before money is committed, so a weak assumption is found on paper rather than in the market; it is the document a lender and an investor decide from, so without a credible one the finance may not arrive at all; and it gives targets that make a disappointing month a measurable shortfall rather than a feeling. Then the other side. Every figure in it is an assumption about an unknown future, and the person writing it wants the business to happen, which is not a neutral position from which to estimate demand. Conditions move, so a plan written months earlier can describe a market that no longer exists. Above all, execution is what converts a plan into a business: a well-written plan and a poorly run operation produce a failed business with good documentation. Other factors deserve weighing against it — the finance actually available, the strength of the competition, the timing of entry, and the experience of the people. Reach a judgement that says what the answer depends on: planning matters most where costs are high and irreversible and least where the business can be started cheaply and adjusted, and support it from the context rather than restating both sides.

flashcards.front: What is a business plan?
flashcards.back: A written document setting out the objectives of a business, the strategy for reaching them and the financial forecasts behind it. It is used both to guide the business and to obtain finance.

flashcards.front: What are the two uses of a business plan?
flashcards.back: Internal — it forces assumptions to be stated and costed before money is committed, and becomes the benchmark results are measured against. External — it is the document a lender or investor decides from.

flashcards.front: What does a lender look for in a business plan that an equity investor does not?
flashcards.back: Evidence the repayments can be met, and security it could claim if they are not. A lender's return is fixed, so growth adds nothing to it; an investor reads the same plan for the size of the opportunity.

flashcards.front: Name the three internal sources of finance.
flashcards.back: Owner's capital (personal savings), retained profit, and the sale of assets. All three come from the business or its owner rather than from an outside provider.

flashcards.front: What is retained profit?
flashcards.back: Profit remaining after tax and dividends have been paid, which the business keeps to reinvest rather than distributing to its owners.

flashcards.front: Retained profit charges no interest. Why is it not free?
flashcards.back: Because of its opportunity cost: the money could have been distributed to owners or used elsewhere. $36,000 retained would have returned $1,800 at 5% a year, so the reinvestment must beat that to be worth making.

flashcards.front: Why might a start-up struggle to get a bank loan?
flashcards.back: It has no trading history to evidence that repayments can be met and usually no assets to offer as security. A bank's return is fixed, so it cannot be paid for taking that risk.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a source and a method of finance?
flashcards.back: A source is WHO provides the money — family and friends, banks, peer-to-peer, business angels, crowd funding, other businesses. A method is the FORM it takes — a loan, share capital, venture capital, an overdraft, leasing, trade credit, a grant.

flashcards.front: What is a business angel?
flashcards.back: A wealthy individual investing personal money in a young business in exchange for a shareholding, usually bringing industry experience and contacts with the money. The investment is never repaid.

flashcards.front: What is venture capital?
flashcards.back: Share capital from a fund that invests in businesses with high growth potential, in larger amounts than an angel and usually taking a substantial stake and a say in decisions.

flashcards.front: What is crowd funding?
flashcards.back: Raising small amounts from a large number of people, usually through an online campaign. Backers may receive shares, a reward, or the product itself before it is made.

flashcards.front: How does peer-to-peer funding differ from crowd funding?
flashcards.back: Peer-to-peer is lending: a platform matches the business with many individual lenders and the money is repaid with interest. Crowd funding backers may instead receive shares, a reward or the product.

flashcards.front: What do family and friends, and other businesses, have in common as sources of finance?
flashcards.back: Both provide money for reasons that are not purely financial — backing a person, or buying a trading relationship — so the terms are ones no commercial provider would match.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a bank loan and an overdraft?
flashcards.back: A loan is a fixed sum repaid in instalments over an agreed term, so it is plannable and suits a long-term purchase. An overdraft covers spending beyond the balance up to a limit, is charged only on what is used, and is repayable on demand.

flashcards.front: What is share capital, and what makes it different from every borrowing method?
flashcards.back: Money raised by issuing shares: the investor pays and receives part of the ownership. It is never repaid, and in exchange the shareholder takes a share of the profits and a say in decisions.

flashcards.front: What is the main advantage of leasing over buying?
flashcards.back: It avoids a large payment at the start — $900 a month rather than $40,000 at once — and usually includes maintenance. The cost is a higher total: $43,200 over 48 months, $3,200 more than buying.

flashcards.front: What is trade credit?
flashcards.back: A supplier agreeing to be paid later. At 60 days on $15,000 of deliveries a month, up to $30,000 of stock is held before cash leaves. Interest-free, but early-payment discounts are given up.

flashcards.front: What is a grant, and what is the catch?
flashcards.back: Money that need not be repaid, usually from a government or development agency. It is restricted to the purpose it was awarded for, carries conditions, and is competitive and slow to obtain.

flashcards.front: What four questions decide whether a source of finance is suitable?
flashcards.back: What is it for? How much is needed? Over what time period? And what cost to control is acceptable? There is no best source — only one that suits these circumstances.

flashcards.front: What is a sole trader?
flashcards.back: A business with one owner who is not legally separate from it. The owner keeps all the profit, makes every decision, and carries every debt personally.

flashcards.front: What is a private limited company (Ltd)?
flashcards.back: A separate legal entity owned by shareholders, which owns assets and owes debts in its own name. Its shares are sold privately, to people the existing owners approve, never to the public.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between an Ltd and a plc?
flashcards.back: An Ltd sells shares privately to approved buyers. A plc may offer its shares to the public, which is what allows a stock market flotation and the far larger sums that come with it.

flashcards.front: What is franchising?
flashcards.back: A franchisee pays an initial fee and continuing royalties to trade under a franchisor's brand and proven business model, giving up independence over pricing, products and suppliers in exchange for lower risk.

flashcards.front: Why is franchising a source of finance for the franchisor?
flashcards.back: Because the network grows on the franchisees' capital: each outlet is paid for by the operator who opens it, so the brand expands without financing every site itself.

flashcards.front: What is a social enterprise?
flashcards.back: A business that trades to achieve a social or environmental aim, reinvesting most of its surplus into that purpose rather than distributing it to owners. It earns revenue by selling — it is not a charity.

flashcards.front: What are lifestyle businesses and online businesses?
flashcards.back: A lifestyle business is run at the scale that suits the owner rather than the largest possible, so it declines growth. An online business trades through a website or platform rather than premises: lower start-up costs, a wider market, immediate competition.

flashcards.front: What is stock market flotation?
flashcards.back: Listing a company's shares on a stock exchange so that anyone may buy them. It raises large sums and lets existing shareholders sell, at the cost of public reporting and ownership open to buyers nobody chose.

flashcards.front: What does dilution actually reduce?
flashcards.back: The percentage held, never the number of shares held. The founder kept all 120,000 shares while going from 100% to 80% to 40%, because the total in issue grew to 150,000 and then 300,000.

flashcards.front: What is unlimited liability?
flashcards.back: The owner is not legally separate from the business, so is personally responsible for its debts in full. The amount at risk is the size of the debt, not the size of the investment.

flashcards.front: What is limited liability?
flashcards.back: A shareholder can lose no more than the amount paid for their shares, because the company owes its debts in its own name. It is what makes investing in a business you do not run possible at all.

flashcards.front: What is a personal guarantee, and why does it matter?
flashcards.back: A promise by an owner to pay a company debt personally if the company does not. Banks commonly require one from a small company's owner, which sets limited liability aside for that debt.

flashcards.front: Which sources of finance are closed to an unlimited liability business?
flashcards.back: Every equity source — business angels, venture capital, flotation — because there are no shares to sell. It can use owner's capital, retained profit, secured borrowing, overdrafts, leasing and trade credit.

flashcards.front: Trace the chain from a business plan to the finance a business needs.
flashcards.back: The plan states the objectives and costs them → market research evidences the demand → the financial section names the funding requirement → a lender reads it for repayment and an investor for the opportunity → the finance arrives in the form the business's legal form allows.

flashcards.front: Trace the effect of choosing equity finance rather than debt.
flashcards.back: Shares are issued → the money arrives with no repayment and no interest → the total shares in issue rises → the founder's percentage falls → decisions are now shared → the cost is a permanent share of all future profit rather than a fixed interest charge.

flashcards.front: Trace why a start-up struggles to raise finance.
flashcards.back: No trading history → no evidence the repayments can be met → no assets to offer as security → banks decline → no profit yet, so retained profit is unavailable → finance must come from those paid for taking risk: owner's capital, family and friends, angels or crowd funding.

diagrams.title: Retained Profit and What It Costs
diagrams.description: How $48,000 of profit after tax becomes $36,000 of retained profit once $12,000 of dividends are paid, and the opportunity cost of keeping it in the business rather than using it elsewhere.
checklist: Profit after tax shown before any distribution
Dividends deducted, and the remainder identified as retained profit
The arithmetic stated, not just the bars drawn
The opportunity cost named: the return the money could have earned elsewhere
The conclusion: no interest charge is not the same as no cost

diagrams.title: The Funding Package, Debt against Equity, and What Each Method Costs
diagrams.description: How Yusra Foods funded $240,000 from four sources, the single distinction underneath every method of external finance, and the total cost of a loan, a lease, trade credit, an overdraft and a grant.
checklist: Each source drawn in proportion to the amount it provided
Borrowed money and sold ownership distinguished, not just listed
Debt: repaid with interest, ownership unchanged, security usually wanted
Equity: never repaid, ownership permanently diluted
A total cost given for each method, not only a monthly payment

diagrams.title: Finance Appropriate to Limited and Unlimited Liability Businesses
diagrams.description: Which sources and methods of finance are open to an unlimited liability business and which require a company, with the single cause behind every difference: only a company has shares to sell.
checklist: Each source marked for both kinds of business, not just one
Every equity source shown as closed to an unincorporated business
Flotation restricted to a plc rather than to companies generally
Borrowing shown as open to both, with security wanted from the unincorporated
The cause stated once: no shares exist, so no share can be sold

chains.title: How one funding requirement becomes four different sources
steps: Yusra Foods needs $240,000 for premises and a first production line.
The founder can supply $60,000 of personal savings, which is not enough on its own.
The assets last years, so the finance must be long-term — an overdraft is ruled out immediately.
The bank lends $90,000 against the production line, and the balance must come from someone accepting risk without security.
chains.result: Family and friends provide $30,000 and an angel $60,000 for shares — four sources, because four questions had four answers

chains.title: Why retained profit is not free
steps: The year leaves $48,000 of profit after tax.
$12,000 is distributed to shareholders, leaving $36,000 retained.
No lender is involved, so no interest is charged on that $36,000.
But at 5% a year the same money would have returned $1,800 elsewhere.
chains.result: The reinvestment has to beat $1,800 a year to be worth making, which is the opportunity cost an interest charge would have made visible

chains.title: How issuing shares changes who controls the business
steps: The founder holds all 120,000 shares and owns the whole company.
An angel pays $60,000 for 30,000 new shares at $2 each.
Shares in issue rise to 150,000, so the founder's stake falls to 80%.
At flotation another 150,000 shares raise $900,000, taking the total to 300,000.
chains.result: The founder holds 40% — still the largest holding, no longer a majority, so control now depends on other shareholders agreeing

chains.title: Why a legal form decides which finance is reachable
steps: A sole trader and a partnership are not separate from their owners in law.
So there is no company whose ownership could be divided into shares.
So no share can be sold, and every equity source is closed: angels, venture capital, flotation.
Borrowing remains open, but a lender facing an owner with no legal shield wants security or a personal commitment.
chains.result: A partnership wanting outside equity must incorporate first — the form has to change before the finance can

chains.title: Why leasing can be the right choice even though it costs more
steps: The machine costs $40,000 to buy outright, in one payment.
Leasing is $900 a month for 48 months, which comes to $43,200.
That is $3,200 more in total than buying it.
But the business never has to find $40,000 at once, and maintenance is usually included.
chains.result: The premium buys the avoidance of a large outlay, so leasing suits a business short of cash rather than a business short of money

mistakes.title: Confusing Internal and External Sources
mistakes.error: Students list a bank overdraft or trade credit as internal finance because no shares were issued for it.
mistakes.why: The test is not whether ownership changed — it is where the money came from. Internal finance is generated by the business itself: the owner's capital, profit it retained, assets it owned and sold. Everything else is external, however it is structured, because someone outside the business provided it.
mistakes.fix: Ask who handed over the money. If the answer is anyone other than the business or its owner, the source is external, whether the arrangement is a loan, a lease, supplier credit or a share issue.

mistakes.title: Recommending Retained Profit for a Start-Up
mistakes.error: Students answer a question about funding a new business by suggesting it uses retained profit.
mistakes.why: Retained profit comes from trading that has already happened. A business that has not yet traded has made no profit, so there is nothing to retain — and this source is closed to exactly the businesses most in need of finance.
mistakes.fix: Check the stage of the business before naming a source. A start-up realistically has owner's capital, family and friends, a secured loan, an angel or crowd funding, and nothing internal beyond the owner's own money.

mistakes.title: Thinking Limited Liability Means No Personal Risk
mistakes.error: Students write that a company's owner cannot lose anything personally because liability is limited.
mistakes.why: Limited liability caps a shareholder's loss at what they paid for their shares, and against the company's general creditors that holds. But a bank lending to a small company will usually require a personal guarantee, and an owner who signs one has agreed to set the protection aside for that debt.
mistakes.fix: State the protection and then its main exception. For an owner-manager borrowing from a bank, limited liability is far weaker in practice than it is for an outside shareholder who signs nothing.

mistakes.title: Confusing an Ltd With a plc
mistakes.error: Students write that a private limited company can sell shares to the public, or that any company can float.
mistakes.why: The difference is exactly who may buy. An Ltd sells shares privately, to people the existing shareholders approve. Only a plc may offer shares to the public, and flotation lists them on an exchange so that anyone may buy.
mistakes.fix: Match the form to the finance the question needs. If the answer involves the public buying shares, the business must already be — or must become — a plc.

mistakes.title: Not Matching the Finance to the Need
mistakes.error: Students recommend a source without reference to what it is for, how much is needed or how long it is needed for.
mistakes.why: Suitability is what the specification asks for, and it is decided by four things: the purpose, the amount, the time period, and the acceptable cost to control. Using an overdraft for a long-term purchase is the classic error, because the facility is repayable on demand and can be withdrawn before the asset has earned anything back.
mistakes.fix: Name the circumstance that decides it before naming the source. Two sources compared against the business's actual need beat five sources listed.

mistakes.title: Calling Retained Profit Free
mistakes.error: Students argue that retained profit is the cheapest source of finance because no interest is charged on it.
mistakes.why: No interest is not no cost. The money could have been distributed to the owners or used elsewhere, and that forgone alternative is its opportunity cost. This is why a profitable business still borrows: if a loan costs less than the return the money can earn inside the business, using retained profit instead is the more expensive choice.
mistakes.fix: Price the alternative. Saying what the money would have earned elsewhere turns an assertion about cheapness into a comparison a judgement can rest on.

mistakes.title: Thinking Dilution Takes Shares Away
mistakes.error: Students write that a founder "lost shares" when an investor bought a stake.
mistakes.why: The founder holds exactly the same number of shares before and after. What changed is the total in issue, so the same holding is now a smaller proportion of a larger company. Dilution is arithmetic on the denominator, not a transfer.
mistakes.fix: Work it from the share counts: the holding divided by the new total in issue. Using the old total is the error a Calculate question on dilution is testing for.

mistakes.title: Treating a Source as a Method
mistakes.error: Students answer "name a method of finance" with "business angel", or "name a source" with "overdraft".
mistakes.why: The specification asks two separate questions. A source is the party providing the money — family and friends, banks, peer-to-peer funding, business angels, crowd funding, other businesses. A method is the arrangement it arrives under — a loan, share capital, venture capital, an overdraft, leasing, trade credit, a grant.
mistakes.fix: Name a party for a source and an arrangement for a method. A bank is a source that offers three of the methods, which is why one cannot be substituted for the other.
